title: The Lost Land Beneath the Sea
summary:
Imagine a land nearly the size of North America, hidden under the sea. Geographer Jerome E. Dobson calls it Aquaterra, a name he first proposed in 1999. In a 2014 paper called Aquaterra Incognita, he argued that this 22.5-million-square-kilometer landmass once hosted some of the earliest human communities — and that much of our history may lie beneath the waves.

During ice ages, huge amounts of water froze into glaciers and ice sheets, so sea levels dropped and exposed lowlands that are now underwater. Those lowlands were full of life: grasslands, wetlands, forests, and estuaries that drew wildlife — and people. Much human progress happened while seacoasts were low, Dobson notes. Early humans lived on such land for the better part of 120,000 years, he argues.

When the glaciers melted, the seas rose again and swallowed those settlements. That does not mean the story ends there. Dobson notes that Jericho is known to have existed when sea levels were about 50 meters lower than today, so finding cities at that depth would not change the timeline of human progress. What could change it, he says, is the possibility that earlier versions of major inventions — he mentions pottery as one example — lie at even lower depths.

Recent discoveries support the idea. In 2021, researchers Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith described seven projects in North America that found traces of life before European contact, now beneath the shelf. One project in the Gulf of Mexico's paleo-Sabine River turned up charred wood, seeds, fish scales, and bones, some dating back 9,000 years. In Belize, researchers found the outlines of pole-and-thatch buildings that had been Maya salt works. Other finds included stone tools and a stone artifact more than 12,000 years old.
why_it_matters: If traces of the earliest human communities lie beneath the sea, the story of how people lived, invented, and spread may be far older and wider than the history found on dry land — and exploring Aquaterra could rewrite what we know about our own past.

background_read: Aquaterra is the name for a huge area of land that is now under the sea, once dry land where early people may have lived.

During ice ages, so much water was frozen into glaciers that sea levels fell and low, flat land along the coasts was exposed, full of grasslands, wetlands, and forests where people and animals could live.
When the ice melted, the seas rose again and covered those settlements, so traces of early human life may now lie on the sea floor.

Researchers keep finding signs of that lost world underwater, such as tools, building outlines, and remains of plants and animals, which support the idea that much of our early history is hidden beneath the waves.

└─ WHEN: Early humans lived on such land for the better part of 120,000 years; finds date back 9,000 years and more than 12,000 years.
